Percentages, Profit & Loss, Discount.blurb: Every percentage problem is a multiplication in disguise. Decide the base, then multiply.

cards.t:
Increase by r% → multiply by (1 + r/100). Decrease by r% → multiply by (1 − r/100).
Successive changes multiply: +20% then −20% gives 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall, not zero.
Net change = (product of multipliers) − 1. Order never matters for the final value.

'A is 25% more than B' → A = 1.25B, so B is 20% less than A (0.25/1.25). The percentage always refers to the quantity after 'than' or 'of'.
Rule of thumb: if X is p% more than Y, then Y is p/(100 + p) × 100 % less than X. If X is p% less than Y, then Y is p/(100 − p) × 100 % more than X.

Profit% = (SP − CP)/CP × 100. Loss% likewise on CP. Always measure on cost unless the question says otherwise.
Discount is on marked price: SP = MP × (1 − d/100). Markup is on cost: MP = CP × (1 + m/100).
Overall: SP/CP = (1 + m/100)(1 − d/100). If this is above 1 you gain.

A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost and offers a 25% discount. Profit?
Step 1: Let CP = 100. MP = 140.
Step 2: SP = 140 × 0.75 = 105.
Step 3: Profit = 5 on 100 → 5%.
Shortcut: 1.40 × 0.75 = 1.05, so +5%. No picture needed.

• Two successive discounts a%, b% → single discount a + b − ab/100.
• Same SP, one article gains g% and another loses g% → net loss of (g/10)² %. For g = 10 that is a 1% loss.
• Price up p% → consumption must fall by p/(100 + p) × 100 % to keep spending the same.
• A trader who uses a false weight w instead of W gains (W − w)/w × 100 % from the weight alone.

• Adding percentages that apply to different bases (+50% then −50% is −25%, not 0).
• Applying markup to the selling price or discount to cost.
• 'Percentage points' versus 'percent'. 60% → 35% is a 25 point fall.
Time: about 90 seconds a question. If you cannot find the base in ten seconds, set CP = 100 and compute forwards.

Simple & Compound Interest.blurb: Simple interest grows by the same amount every year; compound interest grows by the same multiplier.

cards.t:
SI = P·r·t/100, and amount A = P + SI = P(1 + rt/100). The interest is the same every year; the graph of A against t is a straight line.
If a sum becomes k times itself in t years, interest = (k − 1)P so r·t = 100(k − 1).

A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ and CI = A − P. Each year's interest is computed on the previous year's amount, so the graph curves upwards.
Half-yearly compounding: use r/2 per period and 2n periods. Quarterly: r/4 and 4n.
Fractional years: for 1½ years at compound interest, compound for 1 year then apply simple interest for the remaining half year (unless the question says half-yearly).

• For 2 years: CI − SI = P(r/100)².
• For 3 years: CI − SI = P(r/100)²(3 + r/100).
• Consecutive amounts in CI have a constant ratio: A₃/A₂ = A₂/A₁ = 1 + r/100.
• Doubling time (rule of 72): years ≈ 72/r at compound interest.

• Reporting the amount when the interest is asked.
• Using the 2-year difference formula for 3 years.
• Compounding half-yearly but keeping the annual rate.
Strategy: for small whole numbers multiply step by step (×1.05 three times) instead of using a power table.

Ratio, Proportion & Partnership.blurb: A ratio compares parts; treat each part as a unit and the rest follows.

cards.t:
a : b = k means a = kb. To split N in the ratio a : b : c, one part = N/(a + b + c).
To join A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5, make B equal in both: A : B : C = 8 : 12 : 15.
Ratios are unitless and comparable only between like quantities.

a : b = c : d ⇒ ad = bc. Direct variation: y ∝ x. Inverse variation: y ∝ 1/x. In many problems use 'ratio of ratios': if A's share is 2/5 of the total and B's is 1/4, convert both to the same denominator.

Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 9. Adding 10 to each gives 15 : 23. Find them.
Let the numbers be 5x and 9x. Then (5x + 10)/(9x + 10) = 15/23 ⇒ 115x + 230 = 135x + 150 ⇒ x = 4. Numbers: 20 and 36.
Always set the unknown as a multiple of the ratio, never as the ratio itself.

Profit share ∝ capital × time. If one partner is a 'working partner' paid a salary, remove the salary first, then split the remainder.
Late joining: use months actually invested for each partner.
Example: A puts ₹20,000 for 6 months, B puts ₹30,000 for 8 months. Ratio = 120,000 : 240,000 = 1 : 2.

• Forgetting time in a partnership.
• Joining ratios without matching the middle term.
• Using the ratio numbers as actual amounts.

Averages.blurb: Convert averages to totals, change the totals, and convert back.

cards.t: Average = Total ÷ Number. So Total = Average × Number. Almost every problem is one of: change a total, change a number, or merge groups.

Replace a member and the average rises by d: new member = old member + n × d.
Add a member: new average = (old total + new value)/(n + 1).
Remove a member: new total = old total − that member; divide by n − 1.
Combined average = (n₁a₁ + n₂a₂)/(n₁ + n₂). By alligation, the group sizes are in the inverse ratio of the gaps to the combined mean: n₁ : n₂ = (a₂ − A) : (A − a₁).
Equal distances at speeds a and b: average speed = 2ab/(a + b). Equal times: (a + b)/2. The two are not interchangeable.

The average age of 6 members is 25. When one leaves, the average becomes 23. How old was the leaver?
Total before = 150. Total after = 5 × 23 = 115. Leaver = 35.

• Average of an AP (consecutive numbers) = (first + last)/2 = middle term.
• Average of first n natural numbers = (n + 1)/2; of the first n odd numbers = n.
• If every term changes by k, the average changes by k.

• Using n instead of n − 1 after someone leaves.
• Averaging averages without weights.
• Using the arithmetic mean for speed over equal distances.

Mixtures & Alligations.blurb: Mixing is just a weighted average; the cross method reads off the ratio instantly.

cards.t:
To mix a cheaper item (price c) and a dearer one (price d) to make a mix at price m, write:
cheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c).
The quantity of each is in the ratio of the opposite gap. The same cross works for concentrations, speeds and averages.

Pure content adds: if V₁ at c₁% and V₂ at c₂% are mixed, c = (c₁V₁ + c₂V₂)/(V₁ + V₂).
Track the amount of pure substance, not the percentage.

If x litres are drawn from V litres of pure liquid and replaced by water, the pure liquid left = V(1 − x/V). Repeated n times: V(1 − x/V)ⁿ.
Example: 80 L of acid, 12 L removed and replaced by water, then again 12 L removed and replaced. Acid left = 80 × (68/80)² = 57.8 L.

The amount of the pure substance does not change when water is added. So acid₁ = acid₂ ⇒ c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.
To dilute 30 L of 90% to 60%: acid = 27 L, new volume = 27/0.6 = 45 L, add 15 L water.

• Putting the alligation ratio the wrong way round.
• Reducing by the same amount each time in repeated replacement.
• Using percentages as weights rather than quantities.

Time, Speed & Distance.blurb: Distance = speed × time. Everything else is a convenient way of choosing what to hold fixed.

cards.t:
Distance = speed × time. Convert units: km/h → m/s multiply by 5/18; m/s → km/h multiply by 18/5.
At a fixed distance, speed and time are inversely proportional: if speed rises by a third, time falls by a quarter.

Moving towards each other: add speeds. Moving in the same direction: subtract speeds.
Meeting time = initial gap ÷ relative speed. Catching up time = gap ÷ (faster − slower).

Crossing a pole: distance = length of the train. Crossing a platform of length P: distance = L + P. Crossing another train: L₁ + L₂ at the relative speed.
Example: a 240 m train crosses a pole in 18 s, so speed = 240/18 = 40/3 m/s. A 360 m platform needs (240 + 360) ÷ (40/3) = 45 s.
Downstream speed = b + s; upstream speed = b − s. Boat speed b = (D + U)/2 and stream speed s = (D − U)/2.
Runners on a track of length L meet for the first time after L/(v₁ + v₂) going in opposite directions and L/(v₁ − v₂) in the same direction.

• Forgetting to convert units before dividing.
• Taking the average speed as the arithmetic mean for equal distances.
• Adding train lengths when crossing a pole.

Time & Work.blurb: Convert each person's time into a rate, add rates, and invert to get the time.

cards.t:
If A finishes in a days, A's rate = 1/a per day. Working together the rates add: 1/a + 1/b. Time together = ab/(a + b).
Work done = rate × time. Total work = 1 unless a convenient number (the LCM of the days) is chosen.
Let total work = LCM of the days. Then each person's daily output is an integer. A: 18 days, B: 36 days, work = 36 units. A does 2, B does 1 per day, together 3 per day, so 12 days.

'A is twice as efficient as B' → A takes half the time. Rates are in the ratio 2 : 1.
Efficiency ∝ 1/time. Work done in the same time ∝ efficiency.
Inlet pipes add, outlets/leaks subtract. Net rate = Σ(1/tᵢ). If the net rate is negative, the tank empties.
Work = men × days × hours/day × efficiency. Equate for both situations: M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂.
Divide the payment in the ratio of work done (rate × days worked). If they work for different days at different rates, compute each person's share of work.

• Adding days instead of rates.
• Forgetting that someone left part-way.
• Wages split equally when work isn't.

Number System: LCM/HCF & Divisibility.blurb: Factors and multiples; prime factorisation unlocks every question in this chapter.

cards.t:
Write each number as a product of primes. HCF takes the smallest power of each common prime; LCM takes the largest power of every prime.
For two numbers: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers (only for two!).

• HCF: largest equal groups, largest tile, greatest number dividing several numbers.
• LCM: when events repeat together, smallest number divisible by all.
Remainder problems: numbers leaving remainder r when divided by a, b, c are LCM(a, b, c) × k + r. If remainders differ by a constant gap, use −gap instead.

The greatest number dividing a, b, c leaving the same remainder = HCF of the pairwise differences (b − a, c − b).
Example: 46, 53, 74 → differences 7, 21 → HCF = 7.
2, 5, 10: last digit. 4: last two digits. 8: last three digits. 3, 9: digit sum. 11: alternating digit sum. 7: subtract twice the last digit from the rest.
N = p^a × q^b × r^c has (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1) divisors. Odd divisors ignore the power of 2. Perfect squares have an odd number of divisors.

• Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers.
• Forgetting to add the remainder after taking the LCM.
• Taking HCF of the numbers rather than of their differences.

Number System: Cyclicity, Remainders, Fa.blurb: Powers repeat in patterns. Find the cycle, reduce the exponent, read the answer.

cards.t:
Digit 2: 2, 4, 8, 6 (cycle 4). 3: 3, 9, 7, 1. 4: 4, 6 (cycle 2). 7: 7, 9, 3, 1. 8: 8, 4, 2, 6. 9: 9, 1. Digits 0, 1, 5, 6 never change.
To find the units digit of aⁿ, reduce n modulo the cycle length (a remainder of 0 means the last digit of the cycle).
Example: 3⁴⁸: 48 mod 4 = 0 → last of the cycle (3, 9, 7, 1) → 1.

Reduce the base first: 11 ≡ 2 (mod 9). Then look for a short cycle or a power that gives ±1.
Fermat shortcut: if p is prime and gcd(a, p) = 1, aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p).
Remainder when the number is built from many factors: take the remainders and multiply.
Compute modulo 100. Powers of numbers ending in 1, 5 or 6 are easy; for others find the cycle (e.g. 7 has cycle length 4: 07, 49, 43, 01).

Trailing zeros of n! = ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + …
Largest power of a prime p dividing n! = ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + …
For a composite divisor, factorise and do this for each prime; take the minimum.
Beyond a certain k, k! is divisible by the modulus; ignore those terms in remainder sums.

• Using exponent 0 when the remainder is 0. Use the last position of the cycle.
• Only taking ⌊n/p⌋ for factorials.
• Using the units digit cycle for two-digit questions.

Algebra: Linear & Quadratic Equations, P.blurb: Roots and coefficients are two views of the same equation. Use relations instead of solving.

cards.t:
ax² + bx + c = 0 has roots α, β with α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides the nature: D > 0 two real roots, D = 0 equal roots, D < 0 no real roots.
To build an equation with roots α, β: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.

Express everything in α + β and αβ:
α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.
α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β).
|α − β| = √D / |a|.
Example: x² + 8x + 13 = 0 → α + β = −8, αβ = 13 → α² + β² = 64 − 26 = 38.
If x + 1/x = s: x² + 1/x² = s² − 2; x³ + 1/x³ = s³ − 3s. Use these instead of solving for x.

Remainder theorem: the remainder of f(x) ÷ (x − a) is f(a). Factor theorem: (x − a) is a factor iff f(a) = 0.
Dividing by a quadratic leaves a remainder of the form px + q; use two known values to find p and q.
Look for a combination of equations that gives the requested expression directly. For inequalities: multiplying by a negative number reverses the sign; count integers carefully at strict boundaries.

• Forgetting the sign in −b/a.
• Solving for roots with surds when a symmetric identity is shorter.
• Missing that quotient remainders have one degree less than the divisor.

Algebra: Sequences & Series.blurb: Recognise AP, GP or telescoping at a glance and apply the formula.

cards.t:
Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] = n(a + l)/2. Number of terms = (l − a)/d + 1.
Given two terms Tₘ and Tₙ: d = (Tₘ − Tₙ)/(m − n).

Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). If |r| < 1: S∞ = a/(1 − r).
Example: first term 3, S∞ = 2.25 ⇒ r = 1 − 3/2.25 = −1/3.
For positive numbers: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM. For two numbers GM² = AM × HM.
Tₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ for n ≥ 2, and T₁ = S₁. If Sₙ = 2n² + 8n, T₁₁ = S₁₁ − S₁₀ = 330 − 280 = 50.

Σn = n(n + 1)/2; Σn² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; Σn³ = [n(n + 1)/2]².
Telescoping: 1/(k(k + 1)) = 1/k − 1/(k + 1), so Σ from 1 to n = 1 − 1/(n + 1).
For aₙ₊₁ = p·aₙ + q, either compute term by term or add a constant: aₙ + q/(p − 1) forms a GP.

• Off-by-one: the nth term uses (n − 1).
• Using S∞ = a/(1 − r) when |r| ≥ 1 (it does not converge).
• Treating Tₙ = Sₙ.

Algebra: Coordinate Geometry.blurb: Geometry with formulas: distances, slopes, areas, circles.

cards.t:
Slope m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Forms: y = mx + c; y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); x/a + y/b = 1 (intercept form).
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have m₁m₂ = −1 (or a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0).
Distance of (x₁, y₁) from ax + by + c = 0: |ax₁ + by₁ + c|/√(a² + b²).

Distance = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint = average. Section formula (m : n internal): ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), …). Centroid = average of three vertices.
Area of a triangle = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|. Zero area means collinear.

Centre (h, k), radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². General: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
A line is tangent to a circle iff the perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius.
Line 10x + 2y = 20: x-intercept 2, y-intercept 10, so the triangle with the axes has area ½ × 2 × 10 = 10.

• Sign slips when reading the centre from the general equation.
• Forgetting the absolute value in the distance formula.
• Using slope for vertical lines.

Algebra: Sets & Relations.blurb: Sets are collections; relations are subsets of pairs.

cards.t: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B). Complement within the universal set U: n(A′) = n(U) − n(A). A − B = A ∩ B′.

A relation from A to B is a subset of A × B. If |A| = m and |B| = n there are 2^(mn) relations.
Properties: reflexive (a, a) ∈ R for all a; symmetric (a, b) ⇒ (b, a); transitive (a, b), (b, c) ⇒ (a, c). An equivalence relation has all three.
'a ≤ b' on numbers: reflexive, transitive, not symmetric. 'a − b divisible by 3': equivalence relation; it splits the numbers into 3 classes by remainder.
Number of reflexive relations on an n-element set = 2^(n² − n). Symmetric relations: 2^(n(n + 1)/2).

• Calling '≤' symmetric because equal pairs are.
• Forgetting that 'neither' belongs to the total.
• Counting relations as functions.

Algebra: Functions.blurb: Functions are input–output rules; domain, range and composition are the grammar.

cards.t:
Domain: where the expression is defined. Denominators ≠ 0; even roots need ≥ 0; logs need > 0.
Range: the set of outputs. For quadratics find the vertex; for rational functions think about asymptotes.

One-one (injective): different inputs give different outputs. Onto (surjective): range equals codomain. Bijective: both.
Number of one-one functions from m to n elements (m ≤ n): nPm. All functions: nᵐ.
Even: f(−x) = f(x) (symmetric about the y-axis). Odd: f(−x) = −f(x).

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) — inner first. f⁻¹ exists only for bijections; solve y = f(x) for x.
f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.
If the equation links f(x) and f(1/x), substitute x → 1/x and solve the two equations as simultaneous equations.
⌊x⌋ is discontinuous at every integer. In an open interval (a, b), count the integers strictly inside.

• Using ≥ 0 for log arguments.
• Calling x² bijective on ℝ.
• Applying composition in the wrong order.

Algebra: Modulus & Logarithms.blurb: Absolute values split into cases; logarithms turn multiplication into addition.

cards.t:
|x| = x if x ≥ 0 and −x if x < 0. |x| < a ⇔ −a < x < a. |x| > a ⇔ x < −a or x > a.
For |x − a| + |x − b|, split at a and b and solve in each region; always check the solution lies in its region.
log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log aᵐ = m log a; log_b a = log a/log b; log_{bᵏ} a = (1/k) log_b a; a^(log_a x) = x.

Combine terms, convert to exponent form, solve, then reject solutions that make any logarithm's argument ≤ 0.
Example: log₂x + log₂(x − 4) = 5 ⇒ x(x − 4) = 32 ⇒ x = 8 (x = −4 rejected).
Number of digits of N = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1. For 7³⁰: 30 × 0.8451 = 25.35, so 26 digits.
If log₁₀2 = p then log₁₀5 = 1 − p, log₁₀80 = 4p + 1 − p = 3p + 1.

• Forgetting domain checks.
• Dropping the negative sign when subtracting logs.
• Mixing the base and the argument when changing base.

Geometry: Triangles & Polygons.blurb: Similarity, special centres and area formulas solve almost every triangle question.

cards.t:
Angles sum to 180°; exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. Triangle inequality: the sum of any two sides exceeds the third.
Pythagorean triples: (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25) and their multiples.

Triangles with equal angles are similar; corresponding sides are proportional and areas are in the ratio of the squares of the sides. A line parallel to one side divides the other two proportionally (Basic Proportionality Theorem).
Angle bisector theorem: the bisector of ∠A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC.

Area = ½ base × height = ½ ab sin C = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) = r·s (r = inradius, s = semi-perimeter). Equilateral: (√3/4)a².
Circumradius R = abc/(4 × area). In an equilateral triangle R = 2r.
Centroid divides each median 2 : 1. Circumcentre: perpendicular bisectors. Incentre: angle bisectors. Orthocentre: altitudes.
Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°. Each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360°/n. Diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.

• Using the full side in the ratio when the segment is intended.
• Mixing the inradius and circumradius formulas.
• Counting sides as diagonals.

Geometry: Circles & Mensuration.blurb: Know the circle theorems and the mensuration formulas cold.

cards.t:
Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal. Angle in a semicircle = 90°. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
Tangent is perpendicular to the radius. Tangents from an external point are equal. Tangent–chord angle = angle in the alternate segment.

Perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Distance from the centre to a chord of length c: √(r² − (c/2)²). Two parallel chords: add or subtract their distances depending on which side of the centre.

Circle: area πr², circumference 2πr. Sector: (θ/360) πr². Arc: (θ/360) 2πr.
Cylinder: volume πr²h, curved surface 2πrh. Cone: volume ⅓πr²h, curved surface πrl, l² = r² + h². Sphere: volume 4/3 πr³, surface 4πr². Cuboid: lwh; diagonal √(l² + w² + h²).

Volume is conserved. n spheres of radius r become one of radius R = r ∛n. Surface area is not conserved.
Rolling a sector into a cone: sector radius = slant height; arc length = base circumference.

• Using the sector's radius as the cone's radius.
• Direct versus transverse common tangents.
• Forgetting units for area and volume.

Geometry: Trigonometry.blurb: A few standard values and identities handle the entire syllabus.

cards.t:
sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent. Reciprocals: cosec, sec, cot.
Standard values: sin 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° = 0, ½, √2/2, √3/2, 1; cos is the reverse; tan = sin/cos.

sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B; cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B; sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A.
tan(90° − θ) = cot θ. So tan 35° tan 55° = 1.
a sin θ + b cos θ has maximum √(a² + b²) and minimum −√(a² + b²).
If sin A + cos A = k, then k² = 1 + 2 sin A cos A, so sin A cos A = (k² − 1)/2.

Draw the figure. tan(angle of elevation) = height/horizontal distance. For two observation points, write two equations and subtract the unknown distance.
Example: tower height h, from points 20 m apart in line, angles 30° and 60°: h/tan30° − h/tan60° = 20 ⇒ h(√3 − 1/√3) = 20 ⇒ h = 10√3 m.

• Reading sec as cos.
• Using the wrong side as the hypotenuse.
• Mixing degrees and radians.

Modern Math: Set Theory.blurb: Venn diagrams turn counting questions into region-filling puzzles.

cards.t:
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = ΣA − Σ(pairs) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).

Fill the Venn from the centre outwards: triple overlap first, then 'exactly two', then 'exactly one'. 'At least one' is everything but the outside.
Exactly one of A, B = n(A) + n(B) − 2n(A ∩ B).
A set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, 2ⁿ − 1 non-empty, 2ⁿ − 2 non-empty proper subsets.
For percentages: min overlap = max(0, a + b − 100); max overlap = min(a, b). For three sets minimum common = a + b + c − 200 when positive.

• Forgetting the triple overlap add-back.
• Counting 'at least one' for 'exactly one'.
• Not adding the 'neither' group to the total.

Modern Math: Permutations & Combinations.blurb: Count arrangements methodically: choose, arrange, then correct for repeats and restrictions.

cards.t:
Multiplication rule: independent stages multiply. Addition rule: exclusive cases add.
nPr = n!/(n − r)!; nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Order matters for permutations, not for combinations.

• Repeated letters: divide by the factorial of each repeat count.
• Items together: tie them as a block, then arrange inside.
• Items never together: total − together, or the gap method (place others first, then insert into n + 1 gaps).
• Circular arrangements: (n − 1)!; necklaces (flippable): (n − 1)!/2.

Identical items into distinct boxes: C(n + k − 1, k − 1). With a minimum per box, subtract the minimum first.
Selections with at least conditions: split into cases or use total − unwanted.

Arrange letters of ENGINEER with all vowels together: vowels E, I, E, E (3E, 1I) form a block with 4!/3! = 4 internal arrangements; the block plus N, G, N, R gives 5 items with N repeated: 5!/2! = 60. Total = 60 × 4 = 240.

• Dividing for repeats in one stage but not the other.
• Using permutations where order doesn't matter.
• Counting sides as diagonals in geometric counting.

Modern Math: Statistics & Probability.blurb: Probability is favourable over total; statistics summarise data with centre and spread.

cards.t:
P(A) = favourable/total outcomes. P(A′) = 1 − P(A). P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
'At least one' = 1 − P(none).

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Restrict the sample space to B. Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).
Draw a two-way table; it prevents reversing the conditioning.
Multiply successive fractions with shrinking totals, or use combinations C(good, k)/C(total, k).

Mean = Σx/n. Median is the middle value of sorted data. Variance (population) = Σ(x − μ)²/n = Σx²/n − μ². SD = √variance.
Linear change y = ax + b: mean(y) = a·mean(x) + b; SD(y) = |a|·SD(x).
Expectation E(X) = Σ x·P(x); treat losses as negative.
Fair coin, n tosses: P(k heads) = C(n, k)/2ⁿ.

• Using the full sample space for conditional probability.
• Adding probabilities for 'and'.
• Forgetting that adding a constant leaves the spread unchanged.

DI: Theory, Table Forms & Conversions.blurb: Read first, calculate second: most of the marks are in choosing what not to compute.

cards.t: Check the title, units and column headings before looking at any number. Note whether values are absolute or percentages, and which base the percentages use.

• Estimate: round to 1–2 significant digits to rule out options.
• Compare fractions by cross-multiplying rather than dividing.
• Percentage growth = (new − old)/old × 100; share = part/total × 100.
• A percentage-point change is a simple difference of percentages.
Use the totals (row or column) to recover missing cells. Check by verifying the other total.

km/h → m/s: × 5/18. 1 lakh = 10⁵, 1 crore = 10⁷. 1 hour = 60 min = 3600 s.
Always carry units through the calculation.
When two tables combine (price × quantity), build the product row by row, then total.

• Choosing the wrong base for a percentage.
• Mixing lakh and crore.
• Calculating exactly when an estimate would eliminate three options.

DI: Bar, Line Graphs & Pie Charts.blurb: Charts are tables in disguise; extract the numbers, then do the arithmetic.

cards.t: Read bar heights from the axis; check the scale and whether bars are grouped or stacked. For growth, compute (later − earlier)/earlier. The largest percentage rise is not always the largest absolute rise.
Angle = percentage × 3.6°. A slice's value = share × total. Two pies with different totals cannot be compared by percentage alone; convert each slice to a value first.
Bars and line may use different scales; convert percentages into amounts using the bar values before comparing.
A stack's total is the sum of its segments. Share of a segment = segment ÷ stack total.
1) Read the question, 2) find only the needed data, 3) estimate, 4) calculate if still needed.

• Reading the line on the bars' axis.
• Dividing by the wrong year's total.
• Comparing pie percentages across different totals.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 1.blurb: Arrays of numbers with rules for adding, multiplying and measuring them.

cards.t: Add or subtract matrices of the same order entry by entry. Multiply by a scalar entry-wise. Product AB needs columns of A = rows of B; entry (i, j) = row i of A · column j of B. Matrix multiplication is not commutative.

2×2: |a b; c d| = ad − bc. 3×3: expand along a row or column with signs + − + / − + − / + − +.
Properties: swapping two rows changes the sign; a zero row gives 0; |AB| = |A||B|; |Aᵀ| = |A|; |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix; |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|.
Minor Mᵢⱼ: determinant after deleting row i and column j. Cofactor Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i + j) Mᵢⱼ. The determinant is Σ aᵢⱼCᵢⱼ along any row.
Symmetric: A = Aᵀ. Skew-symmetric: Aᵀ = −A (diagonal zero). Identity: AI = A. A square matrix with det = 0 is singular.
For [1 4; 6 5], det = 5 − 24 = −19; the inverse is (1/−19)[5 −4; −6 1], so the (2,1) entry is 6/19.

• Missing the cofactor sign.
• Assuming AB = BA.
• Using |kA| = k|A|.

Higher Math: Matrices & Determinants – 2.blurb: Inverses and linear systems: the determinant tells you whether a unique answer exists.

cards.t:
adj(A) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|, defined only if |A| ≠ 0. A·adj(A) = |A| I.
For 2×2 [a b; c d]: A⁻¹ = 1/(ad − bc) [d −b; −c a].
For AX = B with |A| ≠ 0, X = A⁻¹B. Cramer's rule: x = Dₓ/D, y = D_y/D, z = D_z/D, replacing the relevant column by the constants.
|A| ≠ 0: unique solution. |A| = 0: either infinitely many solutions (equations proportional, consistent) or none. Check using the augmented system.

Three points are collinear iff |x₁ y₁ 1; x₂ y₂ 1; x₃ y₃ 1| = 0. Area of a triangle = ½ |that determinant|.
Idempotent matrices (A² = A): Aⁿ = A.

• Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix for the adjoint.
• Declaring 'no solution' without checking the constants.
• Cramer's rule with the wrong column replaced.

Higher Math: Limits, Continuity, Differe.blurb: Limits describe behaviour near a point; continuity and differentiability are conditions built on them.

cards.t:
If substituting gives 0/0, factor and cancel, rationalise, or use a standard limit. At infinity divide by the highest power of x.
Standard limits (x → 0): sin x/x = 1, tan x/x = 1, (eˣ − 1)/x = 1, ln(1 + x)/x = 1, (1 + x)^(1/x) = e.
L'Hôpital: for 0/0 or ∞/∞, differentiate numerator and denominator separately.
f is continuous at a if lim f(x) as x → a exists and equals f(a). For piecewise functions equate the left and right limits at the junction.
f is differentiable at a if the left and right derivatives exist and are equal. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not the other way. |x| has a corner at 0; x|x| is differentiable at 0.
lim (x→6) (4x² − 27x + 18)/(x² − 2x − 24): both vanish at 6; factorise: (4x − 3)(x − 6)/((x − 6)(x + 4)) → 21/10.

• Cancelling terms rather than factors.
• Standard limits with mismatched arguments (ln(1 + 5x)/x → 5).
• Confusing continuity with differentiability.

Higher Math: Differentiation & Applicati.blurb: The derivative is a rate of change; set it to zero to find turning points.

cards.t: (xⁿ)′ = nxⁿ⁻¹; (eˣ)′ = eˣ; (ln x)′ = 1/x; (sin x)′ = cos x; (cos x)′ = −sin x. Product: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Quotient: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v². Chain: (f(g))′ = f′(g)·g′.

Tangent at a: y − f(a) = f′(a)(x − a). Normal slope = −1/f′(a). f increases where f′ > 0.
Maxima/minima: solve f′ = 0, then f″ < 0 → maximum, f″ > 0 → minimum.
Optimisation: express the quantity in one variable using the constraint, then differentiate.
Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x. For x² + y² = r²: dy/dx = −x/y.
Write the relation between the variables, differentiate with respect to time, then substitute the instantaneous values. Ladder: x² + y² = L² ⇒ x·ẋ + y·ẏ = 0.

• Substituting numbers before differentiating.
• Forgetting the chain rule's inner derivative.
• Reporting the x-value when the maximum value is asked.

Higher Math: Indefinite Integration.blurb: Integration is the reverse of differentiation; always check by differentiating your answer.

cards.t:
∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ −1); ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C; ∫eᵃˣ dx = eᵃˣ/a; ∫sin x = −cos x; ∫cos x = sin x; ∫sec²x = tan x.
For a linear argument ax + b divide by a.
Choose u as the inner function whose derivative appears in the integrand. ∫x e^{2x²} dx: u = 2x², du = 4x dx → ¼ e^{2x²} + C.
∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Pick u by LIATE: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential. ∫x e^{3x} dx = x e^{3x}/3 − e^{3x}/9 + C.
If F(0) = 0 or a point on the curve is given, solve for C and evaluate.

• Forgetting + C (and then using it).
• Not dividing by the inner coefficient.
• Choosing u and dv the wrong way in parts.

Higher Math: Definite Integration.blurb: The definite integral is the signed area under a curve.

cards.t: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) − F(a). Take care with negative limits and with signs.
∫ₐᵇ = −∫ᵦᵃ. ∫ₐᶜ = ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ. ∫ₐᵃ = 0. ∫₋ₐᵃ f dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f dx for even f, and 0 for odd f. ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx.
Area under y = f(x) from a to b is ∫|f| dx. Where f changes sign, split the interval. Area between curves = ∫(upper − lower) dx.
When you substitute u, change the limits as well. ∫₀^{π/2} sin x cos x dx: u = sin x, limits 0 → 1, integral = ∫₀¹ u du = ½.

• Forgetting to change limits after substitution.
• Treating negative area as positive without splitting.
• Mixing up ln of the limits (ln 1 = 0).

LR: Syllogisms.blurb: Decide which conclusions must be true, using Venn diagrams rather than intuition.

cards.t: Take the statements as true even if they contradict facts. Draw a Venn diagram: universal statements first (All, No), then particular ones (Some). A conclusion 'follows' only if it is true in every possible diagram you can draw.

All A are B: circle A inside B. No A is B: separate circles. Some A are B: overlapping circles. Some A are not B: part of A lies outside B.
Valid conversions: No A is B ⇔ No B is A. Some A are B ⇔ Some B are A. 'All A are B' converts only to 'Some B are A'.
All A are B + All B are C ⇒ All A are C. All A are B + No B is C ⇒ No A is C. Some A are B + All B are C ⇒ Some A are C. Two 'Some' statements, or two 'No' statements, give no conclusion.
If two conclusions are a complementary pair ('Some A are B' and 'No A is B'), exactly one must be true when neither is individually certain, so 'either I or II follows'.

• Accepting a conclusion that is merely possible.
• Using real-world facts instead of the given statements.
• Concluding 'All' from 'Some' statements.

Statements: All pens are books. Some books are cups. Conclusions: I. Some pens are cups. II. Some cups are books.
Step 1: Draw pens inside books. Step 2: 'Some books are cups' means cups overlap books, but the overlap might lie outside the pens circle.
Conclusion I: not certain (the overlap may avoid pens) → does not follow.
Conclusion II: 'Some books are cups' converts to 'Some cups are books' → follows.
Answer: only II follows.

LR: Linear & Circular Seating.blurb: Build the arrangement step by step and place firm clues first.

cards.t: Draw numbered slots. Place fixed clues first (ends, middle, 'immediately next to'). Then handle relative clues. Note whether people face north or south: left and right reverse.
Fix one person as a reference. When all face the centre, left of a person is clockwise from them; if some face outward, their left is the opposite direction.
1) List the people. 2) Mark direct clues. 3) Draw cases when a clue gives two possibilities. 4) Cross out cases that violate later clues. 5) Check every clue against the final arrangement.

• Use initials for names.
• Redraw after each new certain fact.
• 'Second to the right of' means two places to the right, with one person between.

• Mixing up clockwise and anticlockwise.
• Treating 'between' as 'next to'.
• Stopping once an arrangement works without checking if it is unique.

Five people A–E sit in a row facing north. C is at the middle. A is to the immediate left of C. B is at one of the ends but not next to A. Who sits at the right end?
Number the slots 1–5 from the west end. C = 3. Facing north, left is west, so A (immediate left of C) = 2. B is at an end not next to A, so B ≠ 1 (slot 1 is next to slot 2), so B = 5. Remaining D, E fill 1 and 4. Right end = B.
Check each clue again before answering.

LR: Scheduling & Days.blurb: Orders with names and days: use a grid and eliminate.

cards.t: Make a grid of people × days (or slots). Put definite clues in first. Mark impossible cells with a cross to avoid reusing them.

• 'Immediately after' means the very next slot; 'after' means any later slot.
• Use ranges: if A is before B, and B before C, then A is before C.
• Cases: if a clue gives two options, test each separately.
• Count: n people across n days, so each day is used exactly once.
Re-read every clue against your final grid. If two arrangements fit, you've missed a clue.

• Reading 'not on Monday' as 'on Tuesday'.
• Forgetting the cyclic week when relevant.
• Using a clue twice.

Four talks P, Q, R, S are on Mon–Thu, one each day. P is before Q. R is immediately after Q. S is on Monday. Which day is R?
S = Mon. P, Q, R fill Tue–Thu in the order P, Q, R (P before Q; R immediately after Q). So P = Tue, Q = Wed, R = Thu.

LR: Ranking & Ordering.blurb: Chains of comparisons: draw the order and count positions.

cards.t: Write each comparison as A > B and join the chains with common elements: A > B, B > C ⇒ A > B > C. Some people may remain unordered; the question tells you how much is needed.
Total in a line = rank from top + rank from bottom − 1. People between two persons = |difference of ranks| − 1.
If A is 7th from the top and 12th from the bottom, there are 7 + 12 − 1 = 18 people. If a person moves up by k places, the people who were between them and the new place each move down by 1.

• Forgetting the −1.
• Treating 'taller than' as 'immediately taller than'.
• Counting from the wrong end.

In a class of 40, Rina is 12th from the top. Her rank from the bottom is 40 − 12 + 1 = 29. If she moves up 3 places she becomes 9th from the top (and 32nd from the bottom).
Chain example: P > Q, R > Q, Q > S. Who is the lowest? S. Can you decide who is the highest? Not between P and R, so check what the question asks.

LR: Blood Relations.blurb: Draw a family tree from words; keep gender and generation straight.

cards.t: Use squares for males and circles for females. Put generations on separate levels. Join spouses with = and children below.

Father's/mother's brother = uncle; their wife = aunt. Father's/mother's father = grandfather. Brother's/sister's son = nephew. Sister's/brother's daughter = niece. Wife's/husband's brother = brother-in-law. Mother's mother's only daughter = mother.
Decode each symbol first: A $ B means 'B is the brother of A'. Write each statement as a relation, then chain left to right. Mind the direction of each relation.
'The person is the son of my mother's only son' → speaker → mother → her only son (the speaker if male) → his son.

• Assuming gender from a name.
• Forgetting that 'my mother's only son' may be the speaker.
• Reading a relation from the wrong person.

Pointing to a photograph, Leela says, 'He is the son of the only son of my grandfather.' How is the man related to Leela?
Leela's grandfather's only son is Leela's father. His son is Leela's brother.
Answer: brother.
Tip: always start from the speaker and go one step at a time.

LR: Direction Sense.blurb: Maps from words: use coordinates and keep track of turns.

cards.t: Facing north, a right turn faces east, a left turn faces west. Clockwise turns of 90° each: N → E → S → W. Turn amounts add modulo 360°.
Start at (0, 0): north +y, east +x. Update after each move. Distance from start = √(x² + y²). Direction = from the start towards the final point.
Morning: the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the west. Evening: shadows fall east. Face the sun in the morning and your shadow is behind you.
Place the speaker, mark the facing direction, then place others with left and right relative to that facing.

• Adding all path lengths instead of net displacement.
• Mixing clockwise and anticlockwise.
• Taking the object's left as the observer's left.

A walks 8 km south, turns left and walks 6 km, then turns left and walks 8 km. How far is A from the start, and in which direction?
Start (0, 0). South 8 → (0, −8). Facing south, left is east: 6 km → (6, −8). Facing east, left is north: 8 km → (6, 0).
Distance 6 km, directly east of the start.

LR: Coding-Decoding.blurb: Crack the rule from the example, then apply it unchanged.

cards.t:
Convert letters to positions (A = 1 … Z = 26). Compare each pair: constant shift, alternating shifts, reversal, or mirror (A ↔ Z, positions summing to 27).
HAND → JCPF: each letter +2.
Compare phrases sharing exactly one word; the common code word is that word's code. Eliminate known pairs to decode the rest.
Letter value sums, position-weighted sums, product of digits, etc. Test the rule on all given examples before using it.
Does the rule work for every letter and every example? Does it need wrap-around after Z?

• Spotting a pattern from one letter only.
• Missing a reversal step.
• Forgetting Y or Z wrap.

In a code, TOUR is written as RRSU. How would FROM be written?
Compare positions: T→R (−2), O→R (+3), U→S (−2), R→U (+3). The shifts alternate −2, +3.
FROM: F −2 = D, R +3 = U, O −2 = M, M +3 = P → DUMP.

LR: Number & Letter Series.blurb: Find the next term by testing differences, ratios, squares and alternations.

cards.t: Test in this order: constant difference (AP); constant ratio (GP); differences forming an AP; squares or cubes ± constants (n² + 1); primes; Fibonacci-like sums; ×a + b patterns; two interleaved series.
Convert letters to positions, find the numeric pattern, convert back. Wrap around after Z.
Treat the letter and number parts as separate series.
Find the pattern from the majority of terms; the term that breaks it is wrong.

• Checking only the first two terms.
• Missing an alternating pattern.
• Forgetting wrap-around.

2, 4, 8, 14, ?, 32 — differences 2, 4, 6, 8 (an AP of differences). Next difference = 8 → 22. Then +10 = 32 ✓.
Letter series A, E, ?, M, Q: positions 1, 5, ?, 13, 17 → +4 each → ? = 9 = I.

LR: Alphabet & Letter Patterns.blurb: Positions and shuffles: convert letters to numbers and look for structure.

cards.t: A = 1 … Z = 26. Position from the end = 27 − position from the start. Letters between X and Y = |p − q| − 1.
Convert to positions and check for a shared relationship (gaps, reversals, sums). The odd group breaks it.
For analogies (YEAR : RAEY), find the operation (reverse, swap, shift) and apply it to the third word.
'How many letters are immediately followed by …' → write the word, mark each letter and test its right neighbour.

• Forgetting the −1 for 'between'.
• Miscounting after M.
• Reversing the word when the question reverses the alphabet.

How many letters are there between B and C in the English alphabet? They are adjacent, so 0 between them.
How many vowels in DREAM are immediately followed by a consonant? Vowels E (followed by A, a vowel) and A (followed by M, a consonant). So 1.
Analogy: YEAR : RAEY :: SPAN : NAPS (reverse).

LR: Number Operations.blurb: Find the single operation that links the numbers and apply it consistently.

cards.t: Look at the first example, test simple operations (+, −, ×, squares), then verify on every other example.
a·b ± k; a² ± b; (a + b) × c; difference of squares; digit operations (sum or product of digits).
Test each option's candidate rule on all given pairs and discard those that fail even one.

• Fixing on a rule seen in a single example.
• Rules that need a hidden extra step.

If (5, 2) → 8 and (9, 4) → 32, what is (7, 2)?
Test candidate rules against both examples. a·b − 2 fits the first (10 − 2 = 8) but not the second (36 − 2 = 34, not 32). The rule b(a − 1) gives 2 × 4 = 8 and 4 × 8 = 32, matching both. So (7, 2) → 2 × 6 = 12.

LR: Data Sufficiency.blurb: Is the information enough? Decide sufficiency, not the answer itself.

cards.t: Answer the question using statement I only; then using II only; then both together. Do not mix information.
I alone, II alone, either alone, both together, neither. Unique answers mean sufficient; two possible answers mean not sufficient.
For seating or ranking questions, try to draw all arrangements allowed by the statement; if more than one gives different answers, it's not sufficient.
Count unknowns versus independent equations. Beware of equations that are multiples of each other.

• Using information from statement II while testing I alone.
• Calling a statement sufficient when it gives a range.
• Solving fully when you only need to decide whether it is possible.

Question: What is Maya's age? I. Maya is twice as old as Ravi. II. Ravi will be 15 in 5 years.
I alone: gives only a relation, not an age → insufficient. II alone: gives Ravi's age (10) but not Maya's → insufficient. Together: Maya = 20 → sufficient.
Answer: both together are needed.

LR: Statement-Action & Cause.blurb: Judge arguments: courses of action, causes and assumptions.

cards.t: A good course is practical, addresses the problem directly, and doesn't create bigger problems. Reject extreme or unrelated actions.
The best reason directly explains the event in the statement. Options that are true but unrelated, or that contradict the statement, are out.
An assumption is something the statement takes for granted. Test: if it were false, would the statement collapse? Reject facts that merely add information.

• Choosing options that sound good but don't solve the problem.
• Choosing a related fact over a necessary one.
• Judging by personal opinion.

Statement: The number of road accidents rose sharply after the speed limit was raised on a highway. Which course of action follows? (I) Reconsider the speed limit. (II) Close the highway.
I is practical and addresses the cause → follows. II is extreme → does not follow.

VARC: Vocabulary - Synonyms.blurb: Meaning in context: pick the closest word in meaning and tone.

cards.t: Read the sentence and decide whether the word is positive, negative or neutral. Substitute each option and test the sentence.
Latin and Greek roots help: bene- (good), mal- (bad), anti- (against), pre- (before), -phobia (fear).

• Choosing a related but non-interchangeable word.
• Ignoring tone (mild versus strong).
• Picking an antonym when under time pressure.
'Her frugal habits helped her save for college.' Frugal means careful with money. Closest: thrifty. Not 'stingy' (negative) and not 'generous' (opposite).
First fix the meaning of the word, then find its opposite. Check for options that are synonyms: they are traps.
un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, non-, a- often negate a meaning. But 'inflammable' means flammable, so confirm with meaning.

• Choosing a synonym.
• Choosing a word that is unrelated to the meaning.
• Ignoring that some words have several senses.

VARC: Vocabulary - Words in Context.blurb: Fit the blank by logic first, grammar second.

cards.t: Is the sentence praising or criticising? Positive or negative words must match the direction of the sentence.
Contrast words (but, although, yet) signal an opposite; cause words (because, so) signal consistent meaning.
Re-read with your answer in the blank. It should sound natural and logical.

• Choosing a word that fits grammatically but not logically.
• Missing the contrast signal.

VARC: Vocabulary - Meanings & Definition.blurb: Know what the word means, not what it sounds like.

cards.t: Learn words in sentences, with their opposites and a memorable example. Review them regularly.
trans- (across), spec/spect (look), port (carry), dict (say), scrib/script (write), bene (good).
Rule out options that you know to be wrong, then use roots and tone for the rest.

• Picking the word that sounds similar.
• Taking the first meaning that comes to mind.

VARC: Idioms & Phrases.blurb: Figurative meanings: never translate word for word.

cards.t: Idioms do not mean what their words say. 'At the eleventh hour' means at the last moment.
Learn the idiom with a short sentence so you remember the situation in which it is used.

• Choosing the literal meaning.
• Picking an idiom with similar words but different meaning.

VARC: One-word Substitution.blurb: One word for many: roots tell you the meaning.

cards.t: -cide (kill), -phobia (fear), -cracy (rule), -ology (study), omni- (all), -vorous (eating).
Herbivorous / carnivorous / omnivorous; amateur / novice; misogynist / philanthropist; atheist / agnostic.
Find the key idea in the phrase and match it with the root of the candidate word.

• Choosing a word that sounds similar.
• Mixing near-synonym pairs.

VARC: Verbal Analogies.blurb: Relationships between words: state the relationship in a sentence first.

cards.t: Common relationships: tool–use (pen : write), part–whole (page : book), degree (warm : hot), cause–effect, worker–product, synonym, antonym.
Write the relation as a sentence ('A pen is used to write'), then find the option that fits the same sentence with the new pair.

• Choosing a word related to the third word but not in the same relation.
• Reversing the order of the relationship.

VARC: Grammar - Subject-Verb Agreement.blurb: Make the verb match the real subject.

cards.t: Ignore phrases between the subject and the verb ('The box of chocolates is…'). The subject is 'box', not 'chocolates'.
Each, every, either, neither → singular. 'Either… or' and 'neither… nor' → verb agrees with the nearer subject. Subjects joined by 'and' → plural (unless one idea).
Collective nouns (team, committee) are singular when acting as a unit. Words like 'police' and 'people' are plural. Titles and quantities of money/time/distance are singular.

• Matching the verb to the nearest noun.
• Treating single ideas as plural.

'The quality of the apples (is/are) poor.' The subject is 'quality' (singular); 'of the apples' is a phrase. → is.
'Neither the teacher nor the students (was/were) present.' Verb agrees with the nearer subject 'students' → were.

VARC: Grammar - Prepositions & Collocati.blurb: Fixed pairings: learn them, don't derive them.

cards.t: suffer from, interested in, good at, afraid of, depend on, married to, different from, capable of, responsible for, according to.
'Despite of' is wrong (despite or in spite of). 'Discuss about' is wrong (discuss). 'Comprise of' is wrong (comprise).
Test each option by saying the full phrase aloud; the correct pairing usually sounds natural.
• Using the preposition you would use in your mother tongue.

VARC: Grammar - Tenses & Verb Forms.blurb: Time and form: match the tense to the time marker.

cards.t: Present perfect (has/have + V3): connects past with present ('I have lived here since 2020'). Past perfect (had + V3): earlier of two past events. Future perfect: finished by a future time.
Zero/first: If it rains, I will stay. Second: If I were rich, I would travel. Third: If I had known, I would have come.
Some verbs take -ing (enjoy, avoid, mind), others take to + verb (want, decide, hope).

• Simple past with 'since'.
• 'Would' in the if-clause.
• Wrong verb form after a preposition (use -ing).
'A/an' for a non-specific singular noun (an before a vowel sound); 'the' for a specific noun. No article with uncountable or general plural nouns.
After a preposition use the object form (between you and me). Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject. Pronouns must agree in number and person.
few/a few/fewer for countable; little/a little/less for uncountable. Each/every take singular nouns. Many/much follow the countable rule.

• 'Between you and I'.
• 'Less' with countable nouns.
• Missing the article before a profession or specific noun.

VARC: Grammar - Error Spotting.blurb: Hunt for the one part that breaks a rule.

cards.t: Subject–verb agreement, tense, pronoun case, preposition, article, parallel structure, word choice.
Read each part separately; test it against the checklist. The error is usually a rule violation rather than a stylistic choice.
Choose 'No error' only if every part passes. It is correct about a fifth of the time.

• Choosing the part that sounds odd rather than the one that breaks a rule.
• Overlooking the first part.

'(A) Despite of the rain, (B) the match (C) went on (D) as scheduled.'
Test each part: 'Despite of' is wrong; it should be 'Despite' or 'In spite of'. Error in (A).

VARC: Grammar - Commonly Confused Words.blurb: Look-alikes and sound-alikes: learn the pairs.

cards.t: affect (verb) / effect (noun); lie (recline) / lay (put); principal / principle; compliment / complement; stationary / stationery; accept / except.
Principal is your pal; principle is a rule. Stationery has an 'e' like envelope.
Substitute each word into the blank and test the meaning of the whole sentence.

• Choosing by sound alone.
• Using the wrong part of speech.
The opening sentence introduces the topic without a back-reference. Beware of sentences starting with 'This', 'However', 'Therefore', 'They'.
Look for mandatory pairs: a noun then the pronoun that refers to it; a question then its answer; a general statement then an example.
The final sentence usually concludes or states a consequence. Re-read your order for flow.

• Starting with a sentence that depends on an earlier one.
• Missing connectors (however, therefore, as a result).

Sentences: (A) However, these were costly to copy by hand. (B) Early books were written by hand. (C) The printing press changed this. (D) It made books cheap and quick to produce.
Opener: B (introduces the topic; A starts with 'However' and needs a prior idea). Then A (cost problem), C (the press changed this), D (explains how). Order: B A C D.

VARC: Para Jumbles - Odd Sentence & Open.blurb: What doesn't belong, and where do things start and end?

cards.t: Find the main topic using the majority of the sentences; the odd one speaks about a different subject, even if related.
Pick the sentence that makes sense on its own and sets the topic.
Read the paragraph without the odd sentence; it should flow smoothly.

• Rejecting a sentence just because it is difficult.
• Choosing an opening that has a back-reference.

VARC: Reading Comprehension.blurb: Read for structure, not for every word.

cards.t: For each paragraph note the main point in a few words. Notice the author's tone from the adjectives.
Main idea (whole passage), detail (find the line), inference (follows from the text), tone (attitude), application (extend the author's view).
Wrong options are usually: too extreme, out of scope, partially true, or the reverse of the text. Return to the passage to confirm.

• Choosing an option that is true in general but not stated.
• Picking a detail as the main idea.

Passage line: 'Although many praised the invention, its high cost put it out of reach of most families.' Question: the author's attitude is… 
The word 'although' signals a contrast; the author acknowledges praise but stresses cost. A balanced, mildly critical tone fits; an option like 'furious' is too extreme, and 'enthusiastic' ignores the contrast.
